The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 9 \\ -2 & -8\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 9 \\ -2 & -8\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot (-8)-9\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}-8 & -9 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} & \frac{3}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} & \frac{3}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot (-4)-(-2)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=-3{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2},$ we obtain 

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

[x]B=PC→B[x]C.

PC→B=PB→C−1=[13−2−4]−1=11⋅(−4)−(−2)⋅3[−4−321]=[−2−32112]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given the Inverse Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ to $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=-3{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot (-4)-(-2)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=-3{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2},$ we obtain 

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $C$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -7 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 4 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 4 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in Another Basis
content.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $C$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
content.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -7 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 4 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 4 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
